cases.intent: The easy case. Everything is stated: dates on every row, report time printed, local times, a rollover marker, and header totals that reconcile. If a system cannot read this one, nothing else it does matters.

raised.statement: A 16h52 duty, four sectors, starting at 05:40 local — you'll be awake from about 03:40 local until past midnight, roughly 21 hours, with the last sector landing at 22:02. No sleep plan makes that duty feel short.

Home standby 06:00-13:00 local, then report 23:00 local the same day for an all-night MAD-ARN-MAD finishing 09:10 the next morning. Only 10 hours between standby release and report, and the sleep you need in that gap is a daytime sleep after you've already been up since 04:30.
AU342 lands at 02:31 local and you're off duty at 03:01 — the whole last sector sits inside the 02:00-06:00 body-time trough after a 13h46 day.

You block in at 03:01 local on the 11th and report at 05:40 local on the 12th. The calendar shows a day off in between, but the body clock has to move about nine hours in one go — it can't, so the 11th has to be split into two sleeps.
Off duty 21:43 local on the 1st, report 07:45 local on the 2nd. With 55 minutes each way to MAD that's about 8h10 actually at home and realistically 6h30 in bed, in front of a 10h09 duty to ARN.
AU837 from DUB lands at 05:11 local after a 14h16 duty — approach and landing right at the bottom of the circadian dip, having been awake since about 12:00 the previous day.
An 04:35 local report means an alarm at about 02:35 and leaving home at 03:40. You cannot sleep enough before that no matter how early you go to bed, and it opens a 12h06 four-sector day.
05:05 local reports on both the 29th and the 30th, and the 29th only ends at 12:15 local — the second early start is flown on a night that starts at 20:00 with an alarm at 03:05.
Duty on the 27th ends 00:56 local on the 28th, then a 05:05 report on the 29th. The single day off has to absorb a late finish and set up an early start, which is two opposite demands.

The two SBY lines show a MAD-MAD sector and a duty window but do not say whether it is home standby or airport standby. I have planned for home standby with the option of getting to MAD, and I have taken the report time as the start of the window with no reporting offset applied.
AU596 appears twice with different routings (MAD-FCO on 12/09, ARN-MAD on 16/09), as do AU445, AU316 and AU690. I have read them exactly as printed, but it is worth a glance before the day.

15h01 across four sectors with an 06:10 local report, and the same pattern again on 05/09 (14h14), 19/09 (14h16) and 24/09 (14h16) — four duties over fourteen hours in the month, three of them off early reports.

raised.statement: The BCN day duty ends 14:54 local and you report again at 00:55 local — about 10 hours door-to-door, of which the commute takes nearly two, so the only sleep available is an evening nap.
MD882/MD826 (report 00:55, off blocks 07:58 local) sits entirely across 02:00–06:00 body time, with no acclimatisation credit and no prior night sleep.

You block in from the Dublin night at 07:58 local and report for the LHR duty at 18:30 the same day — roughly 10 hours at home, all of it in daylight, chasing sleep your body clock does not want to give.
16h11 duty, four sectors, report 14:40 and off duty 06:51 the next morning — the last sector ARN–MAD flies right through 02:00–06:00 body time at the end of a very long day.
The 12th is printed as LIB but you are on duty until 06:51 local that morning, so the day off is really a recovery day and gives you no useful rest credit.
Report 06:10 on the 7th then 05:40 on the 8th, and the 8th is a four-sector 12h07 duty — the sleep before it is capped at about seven hours no matter how well you plan it.
16h56 duty, four sectors, starting from an 05:05 report — the pre-duty sleep has to end at 03:15 local, which realistically means seven hours at best against a seventeen-hour day.
A 14h03 duty finishing at 04:43 local follows the 16h56 duty of the 18th with only about 16h39 between them — two WOCL-crossing days back to back with one short night in the middle.

You finish at 02:55 local on the 22nd and report at 04:35 local on the 23rd — about 25h40 apart — and the 23rd is a 17h02 four-sector duty, the longest of the month. The single day off cannot absorb that clock swing.
14h07 duty ending 03:22 local on 1 October, following the 29th which finished at 22:48 with about 14h27 rest — and the roster period ends mid-recovery, so nothing after it is visible.

The roster prints local time at each station and gives no UTC column, so every instant here is a conversion: MAD/BCN/FRA/CDG/ARN/FCO at UTC+2 and LHR/DUB/LIS at UTC+1 for all of September 2026. The 1h00 report offset and 0h30 post-flight duty end are inferred from the printed columns, not stated in the document.

cases.intent: Every time is UTC. Nothing on the page says what the local hour is at either end of a sector, so sleep cannot be placed without converting first.

raised.statement: The 22 Sep line carries '+1' on every field (report 00:40Z+1, STD 02:10Z+1, STA 13:50Z+1), which places the duty on 23 Sep — but 23 Sep is printed OFF and the header's 'Days Off: 16' counts it as a day off. I have planned it as a 23 Sep duty; 22 Sep is a GRU layover day.
Read literally as 22 Sep, PW344 reports at 00:40Z just 50 minutes after off-duty at 23:50Z on 21 Sep at GRU — that is not a rest period, it's a coffee break, and it cannot be what was intended.

PW895 reports 20:40Z and runs to 07:10Z, sitting across 02:00–06:00 body time from end to end, on a body clock still set to London after only about 19 hours at home following a 00:15Z arrival the night before.

Two back-to-back 13h40 night duties around a GRU layover of only about 14h20, with off-duty at 02:40 local and report at 17:00 local — one sleep opportunity, taken at a body time that's already out of phase.
Wake around 07:00Z for the 10:10Z report and you are not in the GRU hotel until about 00:15Z — roughly 17 hours 15 minutes awake, ending at 21:15 local in a station four hours behind you.

Standby starts 05:00Z, which means a 04:15 local alarm and leaving home at 04:05Z, roughly 24 hours after landing from Los Angeles with a body clock still eight hours west — the pre-standby sleep is scheduled at what your body reads as early afternoon and will be short.
Between the 09-06 arrival (off duty 00:15Z on 7 Sep) and the 09-07 report at 20:40Z you get one daytime sleep at home between two transatlantic duties, with no night in your own bed at a normal hour.

raised.statement: The 27th is a 16h29 flight duty period with four sectors, reporting at 02:50 local. It starts inside the window of worst alertness, runs the entire WOCL, and is the longest duty on the roster by more than two hours.

Off duty 26th at 16:47 local, report 27th at 02:50 local: 10h03 rest at home base. Take off 95 minutes commute each way and only 6h53 is spent at the house, which is at best 5h40 in bed - and it is the sleep before the 16h29 duty.

Off duty 27th at 19:19 local, report 28th at 05:20 local: 10h01 rest, of which only 4h51 is at home and roughly 4h00 is sleep - and it follows the longest duty of the month and precedes a 13h09 four-sector day.
Off duty 29th at 18:12 local, report 30th at 04:15 local: 10h03 rest, about 4h10 of actual sleep, going into a 14h18 four-sector day.

Four of the five duties from the 26th to the 30th report between 04:15 and 05:20 local, with duty lengths of 12h12, 16h29, 13h09 and 14h18. Sleep before an early start is always short, and here it is short four times with only one recovery night in the middle.

Three duties are full body-clock night crossings: BOS-MAD departing 23:10 local on the 11th, MAD-DXB departing 21:50 local on the 13th, and ORD-MAD departing 21:50 local on the 22nd. Each one puts the descent and landing squarely in the 02:00-06:00 body-time window.

The header claims 17 days off, but the 6th, 14th and 21st are printed OFF while I am actually downroute in JFK, DXB and ORD. Those are layover days, not days off at base, and they do not give the same recovery.

The Dubai trip moves the clock four hours east and back inside 42 hours, with a single local night in DXB. There is no realistic adaptation on that pattern, so the 15th is flown on a body clock that is neither Madrid nor Dubai.

cases.intent: The table runs across two pages with the header repeated, and every time cell carries both local and UTC. Treating the second page header as data, or picking the wrong half of a dual time, both corrupt the month.

raised.statement: The '+1' day markers are hung on the local-time column but printed after the Zulu time as well, so 06:35/22:35Z+1 at SIN reads as either 22:35Z on the 18th or the 19th; the same happens with the 16SEP JFK report (20:20 local = 00:20Z on the 17th) and the 05SEP ORD arrival. I have resolved all of them by flight time — SIN arrival is 2026-09-18T22:35Z.
06SEP is printed OFF, but the ORD red-eye lands at 08:00Z and you are not off duty until 08:30Z that morning, so the 'day off' is really a post-night-flight recovery day.

You are off duty at LHR at 00:20Z on 21SEP after a 15h20 duty home from Singapore across seven time zones, and report again at 10:20Z the same morning for a 12h11 four-sector day. That is 10h00 gate to gate; take 95 minutes each way off it and you have about 6h20 at home and under 6h in bed, at the wrong end of a body clock that is still somewhere over Asia.

Second short night in a row: off duty 22:31Z on the 21st, report 08:35Z on the 22nd — 10h04 minus commuting leaves roughly 6h50 at home, and you start that block already down from the Singapore night.

24SEP, 25SEP and 26SEP report at 04:40Z, 04:05Z and 03:25Z — three consecutive starts inside the window where sleep before duty is short and shallow, each one waking you deeper into the 02:00-06:00 body-time trough than the last.

25SEP is a 13h17 duty from an 04:05Z report ending at 17:22Z, and you report again at 03:25Z on the 26th. That is 10h03 rest; after 3h10 of commuting you get about 6h00 in bed, then fly four sectors starting at 04:25 local.

You come off duty at 13:22Z on the 26th having woken at 01:20Z, and report again at 23:25Z the same day for an FCO night duty that lands at 06:22Z — the whole sector sits in the 02:00-06:00 body-time window, on the back of a week of dawn starts.

The simulator reports at 07:00Z on the 28th, about 24 hours after finishing a night duty at 06:52Z on the 27th — you have to flip from back-of-clock to a 06:00 local alarm with one night in between, and a check ride is not the place to be doing that.

raised.statement: A 14h53 duty with four sectors that reports at 15:25 and lands at 05:48 local. The last two sectors — MAD-FCO off at 23:55 and FCO-MAD off at 03:23 — sit right through 02:00 to 06:00 body time, which is the worst of it, and they come after you have already been on duty for eight hours.

A 05:05 report after six consecutive days off. Six days of unrestricted sleep will have drifted your bedtime late, and the alarm has to go at about 03:00 local to clear an 85-minute commute. Realistically you get six hours, not eight.

05:40 on the 22nd followed by 04:35 on the 23rd. The alarm on the 23rd is at roughly 02:40 local, which is inside the circadian low, and you have to fall asleep at 20:00 the evening before to get anywhere near seven hours. Sleep onset that early is genuinely hard and often fails.

You report at 04:35 on the 23rd and then finish at 00:14 on the 25th. That is roughly a twenty-hour swing in report-to-release timing across two days, with only the single night of the 23rd to turn the clock around.

Singapore is six hours ahead of Madrid and you have about 26 hours on the ground. There is nowhere near enough time to shift the body clock, and trying to would leave you half-adapted in both directions for the 13h30 sector home.

Both eastbound returns — CR706 out of ORD at 21:50 local and CR345 out of JFK at 23:10 local — are effectively all-nighters landing in Madrid in the early afternoon. Without a substantial afternoon nap down-route you would be approaching 24 hours of continuous wakefulness at top of descent.
Flight number CR893 appears twice with different routings — MAD-DUB on the 23rd and MAD-LIS on the 24th. One of the two is almost certainly a roster typo. I have transcribed both as printed.

The roster does not state a reporting offset. I derived it from the printed data: 90 minutes before STD on the long-haul duties and 60 minutes on the short-haul ones, with release at STA plus 30. It reconciles against every printed duty total, but it is an inference.

No FTL scheme or operator rule set was provided with this roster, so the conflicts above are flagged on fatigue-science grounds — circadian low, sleep opportunity, continuous wakefulness — and not against any specific regulatory limit.

raised.statement: Off duty at 19:40 local on 03/11 after a 15h30 duty from Singapore, then report 05:40 local on 04/11 — 10h00 between duties at home base, which is less than both 12 hours and the length of the preceding duty. With an 85-minute commute each way the actual sleep opportunity in bed is about 6 hours, taken while my body is still part-way on Singapore time.

Second consecutive early start — 05:40 report on 04/11 followed by a 05:00 standby start on 05/11, then 05:05 on 09/11. Each one means waking at 03:00-04:15 local, inside the 02:00-06:00 body-clock trough, on the back of a long-haul block.
Four flight duty periods of 15h30 report-to-off-duty (29/10, 31/10, 01/11, 03/11) on the Singapore rotations, well beyond any unaugmented maximum FDP.
DXB-MAD reports at 21:40 local and runs to 04:40 local — the entire duty sits inside the 02:00-06:00 window, and it is the second night duty in three days after the 21/10 outbound.

BOG-MAD is a 12h15 duty finishing at 02:30 local Madrid, landing at the circadian low after a westward nightstop where the body is still on home time — the arrival is effectively 08:30 on my internal clock but I will have been awake since 07:00 Bogotá.

A 9-hour standby from 05:00 local, with a callout at any point counting toward the subsequent FDP — a late callout on 05/11 would push the day well past the sleep I have budgeted for the Bogotá departure on 06/11.

The roster prints report 1h30 before STD on all long-haul sectors but only 1h00 before STD on the FCO and LHR turnarounds (04/11 and 09/11), and does not state the reporting rule anywhere. I have used the printed report times as given.

The 06SEP standby releases at 00:00Z (02:00 local) and the MAD-BOS report is 06:55Z; after two 95-minute commutes that leaves about three and a quarter hours actually in bed.

19SEP through 21SEP is four duties in a row, each separated by almost exactly ten hours, and every one of them runs through 02:00-06:00 body time; the only sleep available is in the afternoon forbidden zone.
The second 19SEP duty is 14h10 over four sectors, reporting 22:35Z and finishing 12:45Z, i.e. the whole of the night plus the following morning.

CV154 reports at 01:50Z, which is 21:50 local Boston, and lands Madrid at midday — the whole duty sits across the body night.
Both Singapore duties are 15h20 single-sector and each spans the full 02:00-06:00 body-time window; the layover is only about 33 hours, which is too short to shift the body clock.
22SEP is shown as a day off but the previous duty does not finish until 03:53Z that morning, so the first hours of the day off are spent getting home and sleeping.

Sim finishes 15:00Z on 11 September and the next report is 01:00Z on the 12th — 10h00 rest, and the duty starts inside the window of circadian low with no prior night's sleep to draw on.

13h04 flight duty with four sectors from a 22:35 local report; a night start with four sectors indicates around 10h00, so this is about 3 hours over on the face of it.

An 02:07 local finish on the 18th, one day off, then early reports of 05:40 and 05:05 on consecutive days — three restricted sleep opportunities in a row and a rising sleep debt into the week.

Nothing in the roster was unreadable — local and UTC pairs are consistent throughout (LHR/DUB +1, BCN/CDG/FRA/ARN/FCO +2) — but note this month contains no nightstops, so every recovery sleep is at home and every early report carries the full 55-minute commute.

raised.statement: 13/10 is printed as LIB, but the JFK-MAD duty that reported on 12/10 doesn't finish until 12:20 local on the 13th, so the day off only really starts once I'm home around 13:45.

Report is 05:40 local, meaning a 04:15 departure from home and a 03:45 alarm, but I land back from New York the previous midday with a body clock six hours west — I'm being asked to fall asleep at what feels like 14:00 and wake at what feels like 21:45.
Every other duty in the roster reports 90 minutes before departure; 14/10 prints 05:40 against an 06:40 departure, which is only 60 minutes.
Four sectors from an 05:40 report to a 19:59 finish is about 14h20 of duty starting inside the window of circadian low, and the last sector lands at 19:29 after roughly 16 hours awake.

Spain moves CEST to CET at 03:00 local while I'm airborne on DXB-MAD, so the printed 03:10 arrival is CET; I gain an hour on the clock but the duty is still a full night on the flight deck ending at 02:10Z.
São Paulo is a single overnight — about 15h15 hotel to hotel with a four-hour shift — and the flight home departs 16:05 local and runs straight through 02:00 to 06:00 body time.

Standby starts 05:00 local, so I'm awake and potentially reporting at 03:00 body time, and this comes two days after a standby that ran to 22:00 local — the sleep in between has to be moved forward by nearly three hours.
Three duties in six days finish between 02:40 and 05:55 local at MAD (04/11 DXB-MAD, 07/11 BOS-MAD, on top of 27/10 GRU-MAD), each eating the whole of the 02:00-06:00 window.

cases.intent: Activity codes are single characters — a day off is a bare hyphen — and there is an equipment column that is empty on every row. Both invite a reader to see structure that is not there.

raised.statement: Three consecutive early reports (04:40Z, 05:10Z, 04:40Z on 08–10 Sep) each need a 03:30 local alarm because of the 85-minute LHR commute; evening sleep onset rarely comes early enough to cover this, so you arrive at the 11h01 four-sector day on 10 Sep with two nights of accumulated debt.

Duty on 12 Sep ends 23:21Z (00:21 local 13 Sep), the single day off is 13 Sep, and 14 Sep reports at 04:05Z (05:05 local) — the 'day off' is entirely consumed swinging the body clock backwards by roughly nine hours in one step.

Same pattern, harder: 15 Sep finishes 01:10Z on 16 Sep (02:10 local), one day off, then 17 Sep reports 04:05Z (05:05 local). You land in the middle of the WOCL and are due back at report 27 hours later.

17 and 18 Sep are back-to-back 04:05Z reports (05:45 local departures), the second being a 9h16 four-sector Dublin day, with only a 17h17 rest that yields roughly 14h at home once the commute is taken out.
Third occurrence of the backward swing: 19 Sep ends 22:41Z (23:41 local), one day off on 20 Sep, then 21 Sep reports 04:05Z (05:05 local) for a 10h42 four-sector duty.

22 Sep ends 23:33Z (00:33 local 23 Sep) and 23 Sep reports 14:25Z (15:25 local) — about 14h50 of rest, but only around 12 hours at home after two 85-minute commutes, and that single sleep has to carry you through a duty finishing at 03:05 local on 24 Sep.

The 23 Sep duty operates AT797 CDG–LHR departing 00:15Z and landing 01:35Z, with off-duty at 02:05Z — an approach and landing flown squarely inside the 02:00–06:00 local window of lowest alertness, at the end of an 11h40 duty.
25 Sep repeats the pattern: AT369 departs BCN 22:49Z and lands LHR 00:54Z with off-duty 01:24Z, so a fourth sector is flown at 01:00–02:00 body time at the end of an 11h44 duty.
The final duty reports at 03:35Z (04:35 local) for a 05:15 local departure, meaning a 02:25 local alarm, coming immediately after four days off during which the body clock will have drifted later.

The two standby days (5 and 7 Sep) print only an 'Off Duty' time and a duty length, with no start time; I have read them as windows ending at the stated time — 14:00–20:00 local on 5 Sep and 06:00–14:00 local on 7 Sep — and applied no reporting offset, as the roster's 40-minute offset is stated as 'before STD'.
